item.mechanism: High pressure torsion (HPT) deformation at room temperature causes extreme grain refinement and a high density of dislocations, leading to significant hardening.
item.system: HfNbTaTiZr alloy prepared by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of gas atomized powder (AT-SPS-HPT)
item.supporting_observation: Mean grain size decreased below 0.5 μm and hardness reached 410 HV10; LT spectroscopy showed saturated positron trapping indicating dislocation density >5 × 10^14 m^-2.
item.scope_limits: Not tested on samples with high oxygen content or secondary phases; the mechanism is specific to the SPS-processed gas atomized powder which had low oxygen.
item.alternatives_considered: Hot swaging was considered but resulted in cracking; mechanical alloying followed by SPS produced a brittle specimen with oxides.
quotes: The microstructure of HfNbTaTiZr specimen prepared this way can be refined by high pressure torsion deformation resulting in a high hardness of 410 HV10 and very fine microstructure with grain size well below 500 nm.
Severe plastic deformation applied during HPT processing results in many materials into an extreme grain refinement down to the nanoscale.
HPT processing resulted in formation of a high density of dislocations exceeding 5 × 10^14 m −2 .

item.mechanism: Oxygen content above a threshold of approximately 0.8 wt% causes significant hardening through the formation of HfO2 particles and solid solution strengthening, but simultaneously causes embrittlement.
item.system: HfNbTaTiZr alloy samples with varying oxygen content (specifically MA-SPS and MA-SPS-HPT with >1 wt% O)
item.operating_conditions: As-processed states (SPS, HPT) at room temperature; oxygen content varied by processing route.
item.supporting_observation: Hardness strongly increased with oxygen concentration above 0.8 wt%; samples with high oxygen cracked during deformation.
item.scope_limits: The hardening effect is linked to the formation of monoclinic HfO2 particles; below 0.8 wt% oxygen, hardness remains relatively constant.
item.alternatives_considered: Low oxygen content (AT-SPS) allows for ductility and single-phase formation, avoiding the brittle behavior associated with high oxygen.
quotes: Above this value hardness strongly increased with oxygen concentration. This indicates that there was a certain threshold of oxygen concentration in the sample above which it had a significant hardening effect.

It is likely that the remarkable hardening effect of oxygen above 0.8 wt % was connected with the formation of HfO 2 particles with a monoclinic structure, which were detected in MA-SPS and MA-SPS-HPT samples by SEM and X-ray diffraction.
Oxygen incorporated into the HfNbTaTiZr samples caused deterioration of mechanical properties (embrittlement) and prevented formation of a single phase random solid solution.

item.mechanism: Hot isostatic pressing (HIP) at 1400 °C/190 MPa reduces residual porosity but fails to fully eliminate it due to gas entrapment and incomplete dissolution of elements.
item.system: HfNbTaTiZr alloy prepared by cold isostatic pressing (CIP) followed by sintering (HEAP-S-HIP)
item.supporting_observation: Porosity decreased slightly from 6.5% to 4.5% but remained considerable; chemical homogeneity was poor with undissolved Ta/Nb particles.
item.scope_limits: HIP at these conditions does not remove porosity completely; it is less effective than SPS for achieving full density in this alloy.
item.alternatives_considered: Sintering alone or SPS of atomized powder were found to be more effective for density and homogeneity.
quotes: The fact that even HIP processing at 1400 °C/200 MPa/2 h did not remove the porosity completely can be ascribed to a high volume fraction of pores and to filling of the pores by Ar gas used as a pressing medium in HIP processing.
HIP processing had some potential to decrease residual porosity. However, this decrease was quite small and considerable porosity remained in the specimen.

item.mechanism: Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of gas atomized powder at 1300 °C with a high cooling rate suppresses secondary phase formation, resulting in a single-phase random solid solution.
item.system: HfNbTaTiZr alloy prepared from gas atomized powder (AT-SPS)
item.operating_conditions: 1300 °C, 80 MPa pressure, 2 min hold, vacuum, cooling rate ~300 °C/min
item.supporting_observation: The sample contained a pure bcc phase with no residual porosity or secondary precipitates; oxygen content was low (0.12 wt%).
item.scope_limits: This mechanism relies on the low initial oxygen content of the gas atomized powder; it does not apply to mechanically alloyed powders which have high oxygen.
item.alternatives_considered: Slow cooling (furnace cooling) after sintering or HIP leads to the formation of bcc2 and hcp phases.
quotes: The AT-SPS is the only sample with single phase bcc solid solution with no other phases.
Single phase random solid solution is caused by relatively high cooling rate after SPS processing at high temperature of 1300 °C, where all secondary phases are supposed to be dissolved.

The cooling rate after SPS is very high as the sample was cooled from sintering temperature (1300 °C) to room temperature in 3–4 min. Therefore the achieved cooling rate around 300 °C/min is much higher than 15 °C/min.

item.mechanism: Hot swaging at 950 °C causes cracking and specimen damage due to brittleness induced by high oxygen content and potentially insufficient temperature or high strain rate.
item.system: HfNbTaTiZr alloy prepared by CIP and sintering (HEAP-S-SW)
item.supporting_observation: Specimens cracked during swaging even when enveloped in a titanium alloy; porosity was inhomogeneous.
item.scope_limits: The mechanism fails at the tested temperature and strain rate; the authors note that hot deformation might be possible under different conditions (lower strain rate, higher temperature).
item.alternatives_considered: Swaging with a titanium alloy envelope was tried to maintain temperature but failed; SPS was a more successful densification method.
quotes: The cracking of specimens during hot swaging was at first attributed to a decrease of temperature during contact of the die with the specimen.

It should be pointed out that this specimen contained relatively high amount of oxygen (~0.75 wt %), which may have caused the brittleness of this alloy at the given deformation conditions (i.e., temperature and strain rate).
It is also possible that the deformation temperature was too low and the strain rate was too high for the given specimens.

item.mechanism: Mechanical alloying (MA) introduces high oxygen content and nanocrystalline structure, leading to the formation of HfO2 oxides and subsequent brittleness.
item.system: HfNbTaTiZr alloy prepared by high energy ball milling (MA powder)
item.operating_conditions: High energy ball milling for 42 h in Ar atmosphere
item.supporting_observation: Oxygen content reached ~1.07 wt%; XRD showed broad reflections indicating nanocrystalline structure; SEM detected HfO2 oxides.
item.scope_limits: The high oxygen content prevents the formation of a single-phase solid solution and causes brittleness during subsequent deformation.
item.alternatives_considered: Gas atomization (AT) produces much lower oxygen content and avoids the oxide formation seen in MA.
quotes: The MA powder exhibited rather high oxygen content of ≈1.07 wt %, which was ten times higher than that in the AT powder. Oxygen was incorporated into the MA powder obviously during high energy ball milling due to high surface area of nanocrystalline powder particles.
The high oxygen content in the MA-SPS alloy well corresponds to the presence of numerous oxides (mainly HfO 2 ) in the microstructure detected by SEM and by XRD.
They emerged probably during mechanical alloying and are also one of the reasons of the brittleness of the alloy.

item.mechanism: The absence of a fully formed random solid solution (due to incomplete dissolution of elements) results in lower hardness compared to a true high entropy alloy.
item.system: HfNbTaTiZr alloy prepared by CIP followed by HIP (HEAP-HIP)
item.operating_conditions: HIP at 1400 °C/190 MPa without prior sintering
item.supporting_observation: Hardness was only 151 HV10, significantly lower than sintered samples; XRD showed distinct bcc1 and bcc2 phases with different lattice parameters.
item.scope_limits: This mechanism applies specifically when elements are not fully dissolved; subsequent sintering improves homogeneity and hardness.
item.alternatives_considered: Sintering after HIP (HEAP-HIP-S) improved chemical homogeneity and increased hardness, though not to the level of HEAP-S.
quotes: Interestingly the hardness of the HEAP-HIP specimen was around 150 HV10, which was significantly lower value than that of HEAP-S.

It was reported that the high entropy effect may result into higher hardness since various radii of atoms occupying randomly lattice sites cause random fluctuations of potential energy landscape, which hinders motion of dislocations.

item.mechanism: Sintering at 1400 °C for 16 h promotes grain growth and chemical homogenization, reducing dislocation density and misfit defects.
item.system: HfNbTaTiZr alloy prepared by CIP followed by sintering (HEAP-S)
item.supporting_observation: Grain size increased to ~35 μm; LT spectroscopy showed increased positron lifetime (τ2) indicating reduced dislocation density; XRD profiles narrowed.
item.scope_limits: Sintering alone leaves residual porosity (6.5%) which deteriorates mechanical properties.
item.alternatives_considered: HIP was attempted to remove porosity but was less effective than SPS for density; swaging was attempted but caused cracking.
quotes: Sintering resulted in equiaxed and relatively fine grains. The chemical homogeneity was good after 16 h sintering as determined by SEM and EDS microstructure analysis.

LT investigations revealed that sintering reduced dislocation density and also the concentration of misfit defects, which was indicated by increases of τ 2 towards the value of ≈180 ps, typical for dislocations in HfNbTaTiZr alloy.
The sintering caused narrowing of XRD profiles, which indicated grain growth occurring during sintering.
